The Epic go-live. So I basically ran the Epic rollout at Mission Trail. That's how it felt anyway, ha.

Okay, more accurately. Mission Trail Health switched from the old system to Epic in October 2017. The old system was Meditech, I think, some really old version of it, half the ICU stuff was still on paper flowsheets. The whole system went live at once, big bang, all the hospitals and the clinics the same weekend. There was a whole project team for it, people from Epic, consultants, our IT people, the informatics nurses. I was not on that team. What they did was pick super-users from every unit, and I was one of the super-users for the MICU. There were about 40 of us across the hospital, I think, maybe a few more if you count the clinics.

How I got picked is kind of funny. Our manager asked who was good with computers and everybody looked at me because I was the one who fixed the printer. That's honestly it.

Before go-live we did super-user training, a few full days, and then we had to know our unit's workflows cold. The actual end-user classes were taught by the credentialed trainers, but the super-users ran the practice labs on our units, in the sandbox, the playground environment they called it. I ran those for our nurses, and then they added the step-down nurses and some of the float pool because step-down's super-user went on maternity leave. So I trained about 60 nurses in total, I think. Sixty-ish. I made cheat sheets for the drip titration documentation because that was the thing everyone was scared of, and the cheat sheets ended up being passed around to the other ICUs, which I was kind of proud of.

Go-live itself was three weeks of at-the-elbow support. Twelve-hour shifts, me walking around in a bright orange vest so people could find me. I wasn't taking patients those weeks. People were crying, I'm not exaggerating. Med administration, the MAR, the flowsheets, the I&O, the vent documentation, the order sets, nothing was where they expected. I kept an issue log, a spreadsheet, of everything that broke or confused people on our unit, and I think it got to around 150 items by the end of the three weeks. Some were real build problems, like the ICU drip flowsheet rows were missing a couple of our concentrations, and some were just training stuff. I'd send the real ones to the command center and track them till they got fixed. A lot of the build problems I logged did get fixed, which felt good, because a lot of people thought nobody was listening.

I also wasn't charge yet at that point, that came later, I got charge in 2019. So I didn't have any official authority on the unit, I was just a staff nurse in an orange vest telling older nurses where to click. That was its own kind of hard.

After go-live I stayed on as the unit super-user. We had a monthly super-user meeting for about a year, where we brought optimization requests, stuff the units wanted changed. I put in a bunch for the ICU, the sepsis alert stuff later came partly out of that relationship with the informatics team, I knew who to email.

Honestly this is the part of my career I think about the most now. I didn't know clinical informatics was a job when I was in school. The informatics nurses at Mission Trail were like, you should apply when there's an opening, and there was one opening in 2019 but it wanted Epic certification and you can only get that if your employer sponsors you, and they gave it to someone internal from IT. So I didn't go for it. Kind of regret that.

But what I learned is I'm good at being the person in between. Between the nurses and the people building the thing. I can translate what the nurse means into what the analyst needs to fix, and I can explain to a scared nurse why the screen works the way it does. I think that's the actual skill. And I like it more than I thought I would.
